2.text: from the head, with part of the velvet, or one of the dew-claws. Pieces of

3.text: skin covering the nose are cut from fur animals or sea-mammals, and tied

4.text: to the charm-string. Stones of strange form — for instance, those with a

5.text: natural hole through them — are also tied to the string. Occasionally a

6.text: curiously shaped piece of petrified wood or bone is added.

7.text: Taken in connection with the human-like images on the string, the raven’s

8.text: head represents the “assistant” in the upper regions; the wolf’s head, the

9.text: “assistant” on earth; the head of the fox, hare, wolverene, and polar bear,

10.text: and the noses of their peltries, are charms for hunting these animals. Stones

11.text: (see Fig. 249, d) represent the ground upon which the men of the charm-

12.text: strings walk (teˊntin, “walking-ground”). Since the skulls of animals and stones
12.resolved: teˊntin = t, e, U+02CA (stress), n, t, i, n
12.note: Native gloss 'walking-ground' — raised mark after 'te' keyed as stress U+02CA per §4/§5.8 default (raised mark defaults to stress, never apostrophe); confirmed at 4x, mark is a straight raised tick, not a curly quote.

13.text: are used for divining the future, those on the string are thought to be used

14.text: for that purpose by the “men of the charm-string.”

15.text: A wooden image of a dog is supposed to represent the dog belonging

16.text: to the chief master of the string of charms, and is used for hunting-purposes.

17.text: The part the charm-string plays in relation to the herd and the house

18.text: is similar to that of the fire-boards. Both figure in all sacrifices and ceremo-

19.text: nies. When the family want to separate, the charm-strings are cut into as

20.text: many pieces as there are heirs, and a piece is given to each.

21.text: Occasionally, in times of disease, the fire-boards and the charm-strings

22.text: are presented to the spirits as expiatory sacrifices. For this purpose all

23.text: members of the family, one by one, shake their imaginary diseases down on

24.text: their sacred objects, which are spread on the ground to receive them. Then

25.text: the objects are taken away and left in the wilderness. By this act the family

26.text: are considered to have given to the “spirits of disease” all the luck and pro-

27.text: tection they possessed, and they must collect new charms, which is to easily done.
27.note: Printed exactly as 'which is to easily done' (confirmed at 4x: 'to', not 'too') — reads as an awkward/likely compositor slip (expected 'too easily done'), but keyed verbatim per §2.14 (printer's errors keyed as printed).

28.text: Drum. — The drum used by the Reindeer and Maritime Chukchee is

29.text: of the same shape and size as that employed by the Asiatic Eskimo. Its

30.text: form is markedly different from the more southern type adopted in northeastern

31.text: Asia by the Yakut, Tungus, Koryak, Kamchadal, and Yukaghir.

32.text: The southern drum¹ is large, somewhat oval in shape, and has a grip

33.text: formed by four loose bands. These are fastened to the hoop of the drum

34.text: on the inner side. The other ends meet in the middle, where they are tied

35.text: to a small wheel or a cross, which is without other support. When the grip

36.text: is grasped by the hand, the drum hangs loosely, and it may be shaken and

37.text: its position changed at will. The drum-stick is made of wood, and covered

38.text: with skin or with curried leather.

39.text: The Chukchee drum (Fig. 253) is similar to that of the American

40.text: Eskimo.² It has a wooden handle, which is fastened with sinew lashings to

41.text: the wooden hoop. The diameter of the hoop is from forty to fifty centi-

42.text: metres; breadth of the rim, four centimetres. It is nearly circular in shape.

43.text: ¹ See Vol. VI, Jochelson, The Koryak, pp. 55 et seq.

44.text: ² Compare, Boas, Central Eskimo, Fig. 538, p. 602.
